events.credibility_reason: Claim known only from search-result excerpts (preprint not opened, proof unread); no citation, review or journal version in about 31 months; the paper's framing is partly pedagogical ('an example for mathematical research based on contradictory sources') on an unrefereed venue. Not enough for not_credible: no specific error and a restricted twin-prime case is a modest claim.

why: The statement is a single universal non-divisibility claim over pairs of distinct primes, so fixed-prime results (q = 2 via Stephens, q = 3 via Le, p = 3, 5 via Motose 2010, unspecified partial cases in Motose 2009) and the twin-prime family (Hannusch) are restrictions: case. Results about the stronger coprimality form (Motose 2012, the 2025 puzzle-site searches) and namesake problems (odd-order theorem, Feit's character conjecture, Thompson's conjugacy-class conjecture) answer different questions: variant. The Stephens pair 17/3313 refutes only coprimality, so it is no counterexample here and its object role is null. The only post-snapshot event bearing on the statement is Hannusch's twin-prime preprint: case, unreviewed, and doubtful because its content is known only via search excerpts and has drawn no engagement; the close call was doubtful vs credible, and the unread, unopened source tipped it. No event credits an AI system with mathematics; the ChatGPT mention in Liao-Wang-Zhang is unverified, has no systems entry, and concerns another problem.
doubts: Hannusch's preprint was never opened; its twin-prime claim rests on search excerpts plus the author's publication page listing. Le 2012's content and venue rest on Wikipedia's citation alone; marked digested on the assumption it is a journal publication. Motose 2009's exact cases are unknown. The AI search could not exclude an unlisted OpenAI manuscript.
